meta.title: Model Registries and Versioning
meta.thesis: Model Registries and Versioning is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A release team must track which model, prompt, dataset, and eval produced each behavior. By the end, they should be able to build or review model registry card with version, lineage, metrics, and rollback data, measure the ability to reproduce a production answer, and catch the failure where a rollback changes weights but leaves an incompatible prompt in place.

modules.title: Name the whole release bundle
modules.sub: Track model, data, code, prompt, evals, package, and owner as one promotion unit.
modules.summary: Versioning is useful only when it covers every artifact needed to explain and reproduce a prediction.
objectives: List the artifacts in a complete model release bundle.
Explain why model-only versioning is not enough.
Connect prediction logs to registry identity.

blocks.title: The model file is not the release

spans.text: Problem anchor: a churn model starts over-discounting enterprise customers after a Friday deployment. The registry says "churn-model v42," but the team cannot identify the training data snapshot, feature code, prompt template for explanations, evaluation slice report, Docker image, or the alias switch that sent traffic to it.

A real release bundle names the model artifact, data snapshot, code commit, feature or preprocessing contract, prompt or retrieval index when relevant, eval set, metrics, package image, owner, approval, deployment alias, and rollback target. Without that, debugging becomes archaeology.

items.text: Product framing: versioning answers which customer-facing behavior changed and who approved it.
Engineering framing: versioning makes rollback and reproduction a deterministic operation.
Governance framing: versioning records evidence, but it does not by itself prove quality.

blocks.title: Worked artifact: registry card for one release

spans.text: For an LLM feature, add prompt version, model provider or self-hosted endpoint, retrieval index version, tool schema version, and safety eval report. The principle is identical: prediction behavior comes from a bundle, not one weight file.

blocks.title: Registry scope
blocks.prompt: What is the biggest flaw in registering only `model.pkl`?

options.text: It makes the model too easy to find.
It omits the data, code, package, eval, and deployment context needed for debugging.
It prevents all future retraining.

blocks.explanation: The model artifact matters, but production behavior depends on the full release bundle.

modules.title: Make lineage immutable at boundaries
modules.sub: Separate experimental churn from production identities that can be audited and rolled back.
modules.summary: Training can create new artifacts freely; production should consume named versions and aliases with history.
objectives: Explain immutable data and model references.
Describe why mutable paths break incident response.

blocks.title: Aliases are pointers, history is evidence

spans.text: Experiment runs are allowed to be messy. Production references should not be. A release should point to immutable data snapshots, code commits, package tags, and registered model versions. Human-friendly aliases such as champion, staging, canary, and rollback are useful only when moving them leaves history.

DVC and lake-style tools can identify data versions; MLflow-style registries identify model versions and status. Deployment systems then resolve an alias to a version. The dangerous anti-pattern is a mutable path like `models/current.pkl` because it answers today and erases yesterday.

cells.text: snapshot ID, table version, or DVC/lake commit
cannot explain why a retrain changed behavior
registry version, run ID, parameters, metrics
cannot compare or roll back reliably
image tag, alias history, prediction logs
cannot tell which version answered users

blocks.title: Case study: rollback that did not roll back

spans.text: An incident team moves the model alias from v42 back to v41, but errors continue. The registry rollback worked; the hidden problem was that the feature service still served the new transformation code and the explanation prompt still used v42 assumptions. A model rollback without feature, prompt, and package rollback is only partial.
This is the spaced recall from module 1: the release was the whole bundle. Rollback must restore the bundle or explicitly prove which components are safe to keep.

modules.title: Promote with evidence, not vibes
modules.sub: Use gates for metrics, slices, latency, schema compatibility, and human approval.
modules.summary: A registry records status; release gates decide whether the status is deserved.
objectives: Distinguish registry status from quality control.
Define promotion gates for ML and LLM releases.
Include slice metrics and contract tests before alias changes.

blocks.title: The registry is not the judge

spans.text: A registry can say staging, production, champion, or archived. Those labels are dangerous if they are only labels. The evidence behind promotion should include aggregate metric change, slice behavior, calibration or ranking quality, latency and throughput, input/output schema compatibility, package tests, and an owner approval.

For LLM applications, the release bundle adds prompt version, retrieval index, model/provider route, tool schema, safety checks, and eval transcripts. A registry does not have to store all content directly, but it must link to immutable evidence.

blocks.title: Worked promotion gate for churn v42

spans.text: Gate: overall AUC must not drop by more than .01; enterprise recall must improve or stay within .02; p95 latency under 100 ms; input schema unchanged or migration approved; package contract tests pass on 100 golden examples; prediction logs include version 42; rollback to v41 tested in staging.
The approver can now say what was accepted. If enterprise recall worsens next week, the team knows whether the risk was visible at release or emerged after traffic shifted.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Use registry status as a pointer to evidence, not a substitute for evidence.
blocks.useWhen: Promote when metrics, slice checks, latency, schema tests, package tests, and rollback evidence are linked to the version.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid moving aliases because a notebook looked good or a single aggregate metric improved.

blocks.title: Prediction log identity check

spans.text: This code tests the production side of versioning. Registration is incomplete if prediction logs cannot later identify the release bundle that made a decision.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What incident question becomes hard if `registry_alias` and `model_version` are missing from logs?
predictThenReveal.answer: You cannot reliably know which release answered a user request, so rollback verification and root-cause analysis become guesswork.

spans.text: AI-generated MLOps plans often mention MLflow or a registry but skip lifecycle edges. Check whether the plan records data snapshots, code commit, package image, input/output schema, eval report, approver, alias history, prediction-log identity, and rollback procedure.

items.text: Can a prediction be traced to the exact version and package?
Can the team reproduce the eval that justified promotion?
Can rollback restore prompt, retrieval index, feature code, and tool schema when relevant?
Does retention policy say which artifacts can be deleted and when?

blocks.title: Production traceability
blocks.prompt: Why should prediction logs include model version?

options.text: So the model file becomes smaller.
So incidents and metrics can be tied to the exact release that answered.
So retraining can skip evaluation.

blocks.explanation: Versioned logs connect production outcomes back to release evidence.

modules.summary: The learner should finish able to build a release card that supports promotion, incident review, and rollback.
objectives: Recall the release bundle from memory.
Write a retrieval prompt for registry design.
Produce a capstone model release card.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "What must a registry-backed model release record so I can debug and roll it back?" Include data snapshot, code commit, model artifact, package, schema, eval set, metrics, slice checks, latency, owner, alias history, prediction logs, and rollback target.
Spaced recall: a registry is not quality control. It is the place where quality evidence, artifact identity, and deployment status meet.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Treat every promoted model as an auditable release bundle.
blocks.useWhen: Use formal registry workflow when models affect users, money, compliance, or repeated operational decisions.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid heavyweight registry process for throwaway experiments, but do not let experiments become production by accident.

spans.text: Choose a model or LLM feature. Fill in artifact, data, code, prompt/retrieval/tool versions if relevant, package image, eval report, slice metrics, latency, owner, alias, rollout plan, prediction-log fields, and rollback command. Then ask a teammate to answer: "Which version answered request X, and how do we roll it back?"
Next rung: connect this to monitoring drift and quality, where release identity becomes the join key for live performance changes.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: The accelerator environment used to train or serve a model version.
gpu.technicalNote: A release record should include hardware assumptions when they affect reproducibility, latency, or numerical behavior.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: The deployed prediction path that consumes a registered version.
serving.technicalNote: Serving must log the exact model version, prompt or preprocessing version, and alias that answered each request.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The boundary that maps a product name to a registered version or alias.
gateway.technicalNote: A gateway or deployment layer should resolve stable aliases such as champion, canary, or rollback without losing version history.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: A release metric that must be compared across versions.
latency.technicalNote: Registry approval should include latency and resource metrics, not only offline quality, because a slower model can fail production even if accuracy improves.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: How much prediction traffic a version can handle.
throughput.technicalNote: Throughput belongs in the version evidence when batch behavior, hardware, or packaging changes.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: Giving every model, data snapshot, code commit, prompt, and eval set an immutable identity.
versioning.technicalNote: Versioning is the core concept: a registry records artifacts and status, but tests and approval evidence decide whether a version should move.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A team registers a new model version but only saves the model weights and a version number. During an incident, they cannot reproduce the exact predictions from last Tuesday. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The model weights file was too large to store correctly.
The release bundle was incomplete — preprocessing code, the data snapshot reference, and environment spec were not included.
The version number was not incremented properly.
The registry did not support rollback for that model type.

questions.explanation: A model-only registration omits the preprocessing code, data reference, and environment spec that together determine predictions — without them, exact reproduction is impossible.

questions.prompt: Your team uses a mutable path (e.g., `models/champion/latest`) as the production pointer. An incident occurs and you need to know exactly which model version was serving traffic 48 hours ago. Why does the mutable path make this hard?

options.text: Mutable paths compress model files, making them harder to load.
Mutable paths do not record which version they pointed to at any past moment, so the historical link is lost.
Mutable paths require admin permissions that slow down incident response.
Mutable paths only work in development environments, not production.

questions.explanation: When a path is overwritten rather than versioned, there is no audit trail of what it pointed to at a given time — aliases over immutable version IDs preserve that history.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a promotion gate for moving a model from 'staging' to 'production' status in a registry?

options.text: A senior engineer manually approves the model because it looks reasonable.
The model achieves a higher overall accuracy than the previous champion.
The model passes slice-level metric thresholds, a data contract test, and any required LLM-specific checks before the production alias is updated.
The model is registered with a new version number and automatically promoted after 24 hours.

questions.explanation: Promotion gates require evidence — slice metrics, contract tests, and model-type-specific checks — not just overall accuracy or human intuition, before the alias is moved.

questions.prompt: Name TWO fields that a prediction log entry should capture in order to tie a live prediction back to a specific registered model version during an incident review.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any two of: the model version ID (or registry URI), the alias that was active at prediction time, the input data reference or hash, the timestamp, and the prediction output. The key requirement is that at least one field uniquely identifies the registered model version.
questions.explanation: Logging the model version ID and the active alias (or equivalent registry pointer) lets investigators replay or audit exactly which model produced a given prediction.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing an AI-generated registry plan for a new LLM release. The plan includes model weights, a version number, overall benchmark scores, and a 'production' alias update step. What critical gap should you flag before approving it?

options.text: The plan should use a different file format for the model weights.
The plan is missing slice-level evaluations, a rollback pointer to the previous production version, and a data/prompt contract test.
LLM releases do not need a registry — they should be deployed directly.
The alias should be updated before benchmarking, not after.

questions.explanation: A rollback-ready LLM release plan must include slice metrics, contract tests, and an explicit rollback reference — overall benchmarks alone are not sufficient promotion evidence.
